questions.worked_solution:
First, let's define a function $h(t):$

$$
h(t)=({t}^{2}+3)^{2}
$$

To differentiate this function, we use the chain rule. Let 

$$
g(t)={t}^{2}+3,\,h(g(t))=g(t)^{2}.
$$

Differentiating our functions, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{g}^{′}(t) & =({t}^{2}+3)^{′}=2t, \\ {h}^{′}(g(t)) & =({g}^{2})^{′}=2g.\end{aligned}
$$

Then, using the chain rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[({t}^{2}+3)^{2}] & ={h}^{′}(t) \\  & ={h}^{′}(g(t))\cdot {g}^{′}(t) \\  & =2g\cdot 2t \\  & =4t({t}^{2}+3).\end{aligned}
$$

x(t)=\frac{t}{({t}^{2}+3)^{2}},\,t>0

$$
{g}^{′}(t)=1,

$$

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}(t) & =\frac{{g}^{′}(t)\cdot h(t)-g(t)\cdot {h}^{′}(t)}{[h(t)]^{2}} \\  & =\frac{(1)\cdot ({t}^{2}+3)^{2}-(t)\cdot (4t({t}^{2}+3))}{{(({t}^{2}+3)^{2})}^{2}} \\  & =\frac{({t}^{2}+3)^{2}-4{t}^{2}({t}^{2}+3)}{({t}^{2}+3)^{4}} \\  & =\frac{({t}^{2}+3)-4{t}^{2}}{({t}^{2}+3)^{3}} \\  & =\frac{-3{t}^{2}+3}{({t}^{2}+3)^{3}} \\  & =\frac{3-3{t}^{2}}{({t}^{2}+3)^{3}}.\end{aligned}

$$

Now, substituting $t=1,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}(1) & =\frac{3-3(1)^{2}}{({1}^{2}+3)^{3}} \\  & =\frac{3-3}{{4}^{3}} \\  & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the instantaneous rate of change in the particle's $x$-value when $t=1$ second is $0\,\text{m}/\text{s}.$

questions.problem:
It can be shown that the particle comes to an instantaneous rest in the $x$-direction at the critical points of $x(t).$ Find these critical points.

The particle comes to an instantaneous rest in the $x$-direction when $t=$
{{field-1}} seconds.
questions.worked_solution:
A critical point of $x(t)$ is a point $t=c$ in the domain of $x$ such that either ${x}^{′}(c)=0$ or ${x}^{′}(c)$ does not exist.

In part 2, we obtained

$$
{x}^{′}(t)=\frac{3-3{t}^{2}}{({t}^{2}+3)^{3}}.
$$

We now proceed to find the critical points:

* First, we compute the points where ${x}^{′}(c)=0.$ We set the derivative equal to zero, and solve for $t:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{3-3{t}^{2}}{({t}^{2}+3)^{3}} & =0 \\ 3-3{t}^{2} & =0 \\ 3 & =3{t}^{2} \\ {t}^{2} & =1 \\ t & =\pm 1\end{aligned}
$$

However, $x(t)$ is only defined for $t>0.$ Therefore, $x(t)$ has a stationary point at $t=1.$

* Second, we note that ${x}^{′}(t)$ exists for all values of $t$ in the domain of $x(t).$ So $x(t)$ has no non-stationary critical points.

Therefore, we conclude that the critical point of $x(t)$ is $t=1.$

questions.problem:
The acceleration of the particle in the $y$-direction when $t=1$ second is{{field-1}}
$\text{m}/{\text{s}}^{2}.$
questions.worked_solution:
The particle's velocity in the $y$-direction is given by ${y}^{′}(t).$ Therefore, the acceleration in the $y$-direction is ${y}^{″}(t):$

Differentiating ${y}^{′}(t)$ using the quotient rule, we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{″}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({y}^{′}(t)) \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\frac{3-3{t}^{2}}{t({t}^{2}+3)}) \\  & =\frac{(-6t)t({t}^{2}+3)-(3-3{t}^{2})(3{t}^{2}+3)}{{t}^{2}({t}^{2}+3)^{2}} \\  & =\frac{-6{t}^{4}-18{t}^{2}-(9-9{t}^{4})}{{t}^{2}({t}^{2}+3)^{2}} \\  & =\frac{3{t}^{4}-18{t}^{2}-9}{{t}^{2}({t}^{2}+3)^{2}}\end{aligned}
$$

To calculate the acceleration at time $t=1,$ we substitute into the above:

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{″}(1) & =\frac{3(1)^{4}-18(1)^{2}-9}{{1}^{2}({1}^{2}+3)^{2}} \\  & =\frac{3-18-9}{16} \\  & =\frac{-24}{16} \\  & =-\frac{3}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the acceleration in the $y$-direction when $t=1$ is $-\frac{3}{2}\,\text{m}/{\text{s}}^{2}.$

questions.worked_solution:
Our task is to find $A,$ $B,$ and $C$ such that

$$
\frac{3-3{t}^{2}}{t({t}^{2}+3)}=\frac{At+B}{{t}^{2}+3}+\frac{C}{t}
$$

Note that since $p(t)={t}^{2}+3$ is an irreducible quadratic factor, we must use a linear term $At+B$ in the numerator.

We multiply both sides by $t({t}^{2}+3)$ and get

$$
3-3{t}^{2}=(At+B)t+C({t}^{2}+3).
$$

Plugging in $t=0$ eliminates the $A$ and $B$ terms and allows us to solve for $C.$ We get

$$
\begin{aligned}3-3(0)^{2} & =(A(0)+B)(0)+C({0}^{2}+3) \\ 3 & =3C \\ C & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

Plugging in $t=1$ and using our result for $C$ gives us

$$
\begin{aligned}3-3(1)^{2} & =(A(1)+B)(1)+(1)({1}^{2}+3) \\ 0 & =A+B+4 \\ A+B & =-4\end{aligned}
$$

Plugging in $t=-1$ and using our result for $C$ gives us

$$
\begin{aligned}3-3(-1)^{2} & =(A(-1)+B)(-1)+(1)((-1)^{2}+3) \\ 0 & =A-B+4 \\ A-B & =-4\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have the following system of equations:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}A+B=-4, \\ A-B=-4.\end{aligned}
$$

The solution of this system is $A=-4$ and $B=0.$ Therefore, our final result is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{3-3{t}^{2}}{t({t}^{2}+3)} & =\frac{-4t}{{t}^{2}+3}+\frac{1}{t} \\  & =\frac{1}{t}-\frac{4t}{{t}^{2}+3}.\end{aligned}
$$
